---

**In Praise of Error**

Somewhere around the year 1400, in a room that smells of parchment and cold stone, a scribe is copying a poem. He has been at it since morning. His neck aches, the light has gone amber, and the lines of verse swim a little when his eyes travel from the page he is copying to the page he is making. Two lines on his exemplar happen to end with the same word. His eye, shuttling back and forth, catches the second ending where it expects the first and slides—one line of the poem simply ceases to exist in his copy. The mistake has a technical name, *homoeoteleuton*, "same ending," and every scribe made such mistakes, and every scholar who studies old manuscripts knows them the way a doctor knows a cough.

Here is the strange thing: seven hundred years later, that error is the most eloquent thing on the page. A researcher comparing manuscripts finds three copies of the poem that all skip the same line, and that shared mistake proves the three descend from a single ancestor—one scribe's tired afternoon, fossilized into evidence. The flawless parts of a manuscript tell you almost nothing about where it came from; any correct line could have been copied from anywhere. The flaw is the fingerprint. The error is the genealogy. Without it, the manuscript would be mute about its own past; with it, the thing wears its family tree on its sleeve.

The Romans built a pun into their language that I have come to think of as a compressed philosophy. The verb *errare* meant both to wander and to be wrong. An error, in the oldest sense, was not a defect but a detour—a going astray, a drift off the road. (Our "error" descends from theirs by a long road of its own: Latin *error* became Old French *errour*, which wandered into English. Even the word for wandering wandered.) We tend to treat error as a falling-away from correctness, an embarrassment to be corrected. But look closely at how anything alive actually works—cells, words, songs, species, scientific theories—and you find something more disorienting: error is not a falling-away from the process. Error is the process. Everything that grows copies itself, nothing copies itself perfectly, and the whole history of the world runs on the difference.

Consider the most successful copyist on Earth. Deep in every one of your cells, enzymes called DNA polymerases unzip the double helix and, letter by letter, transcribe a new strand—a scribe, essentially, that copies three billion characters without a break. The proofreading machinery chugging along behind it drives the fidelity up to roughly one error per billion letters. And yet not zero. Never zero. That residue of sloppiness—the near-nothing the proofreaders cannot catch—is the entire budget of the possible. Mutation is a copying error. Most are invisible or harmful, some ruinous, a vanishing few useful—and those vanishing few are all that natural selection has to work with. Every trait that ever helped anything survive—the eye, the wing, the opposable thumb, the brain reading this sentence—began as somebody's typo. Each of us is born with a few dozen brand-new ones.

A creature that copied itself perfectly would be perfect the way a statue is perfect: finished, which is to say done. The world would change around it—ice ages arrive, rivals evolve, diseases mutate—and its flawless fidelity to yesterday would strand it there forever. In a world that refuses to sit still, error is the only fidelity available. Even the error rate itself is tuned. Too little error and a lineage freezes; too much and the message dissolves into noise before it can be inherited—what the chemist Manfred Eigen called the error threshold. Viruses like HIV live right up against that threshold, copying themselves so sloppily that within a single patient they exist as a swarm of variants rather than a single strain, and the swarm's very sloppiness is how it slips past drugs and immune systems. Your own body, when it needs to improvise, deliberately turns the error rate up. When you're infected, your B cells mutate their antibody genes roughly a million times faster than normal, generating a library of slightly broken copies, and then hold a brutal audition in which only the mistakes that happen to grip the invader survive. The immune system is a planned economy of error: make mistakes on purpose, keep the useful ones, discard the rest.

Words do the same thing. Language is copied mouth to ear, generation to generation, and the copying is sloppy in exactly the ways DNA copying is sloppy. Sounds drift by tiny increments until *pater* becomes *father*—systematically, lawfully, whole families of sounds shifting together; the philologists have the laws to prove it. But the loveliest examples are misparsings. Old French gave English speakers a cloth called a *napron*; within a couple of centuries "a napron" had been re-heard as "an apron," the *n* defecting to the article—while *napkin* kept it. "An ewte" became "a newt." "An ekename," an also-name, became "a nickname." And the process is running right now, in public, in your own lifetime: English speakers by the million say "a whole nother," having miscounted the *n* in "another"—the same historical mistake, made in the opposite direction, five hundred years later. The old singular *pease* (as in pease porridge) was heard as a plural and forced to spawn a new singular, *pea*. *Asparagus*, a word that looked like it came from nowhere, was hammered into familiar English materials as *sparrow-grass*, which eighteenth-century purists complained about while everyone kept saying it.

When Darwin published his tree of life, the philologists were the least surprised people in Europe. They had been drawing family trees of languages for decades and recognized a cousin's work when they saw it. Copy, vary, select: run that algorithm on molecules and you get biology; run it on words and you get the history of every language you have ever heard. It is also why a living language cannot be ruled by an academy. A language that could not err could not change, and a language that cannot change is called dead.

Back to the scribe. Before printing, every text was a hand-copied organism, and every copy was a generation. The scholars who study manuscript traditions are, in effect, biologists of dead texts, and their central tool is the shared error. A distinctive mistake in three manuscripts is a shared mutation, and a shared mutation proves a shared ancestor. From such clues they build *stemma*—family trees of manuscripts—triangulating toward lost originals. The Canterbury Tales survives in more than eighty manuscripts, and sorting them into families is largely a matter of watching where the copies stumble together. In recent years the biologists have returned the philologists' favor: software built to sort species by their DNA has been pointed at manuscript traditions, and it works, recovering trees broadly consistent with what human scholars deduced by hand.
